title: The Effects of Acoustic Turn-by-turn Navigation on Wayfinding
venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
design: Driving simulator study; compared no-guidance repeated route travel vs. turn-by-turn guided first drive then unaided memory-based second drive; randomisation not reported in retrieved text.
measures: route travel time; assessment of scene recognition
key_finding: Results show that using a turn-by-turn navigation system negates route learning and impairs scene recognition. These findings suggest that using a navigation system while driving creates inattention blindness, a failure to “see” elements in the environment.
caveat_flags: abstract only; sample size not reported; randomisation not reported

title: How Navigational Aids Impair Spatial Memory: Evidence for Divided Attention
design: Within-participants: verbal aid vs. tonal aid vs. no-aid conditions during goal-directed navigation in desktop virtual environments; randomisation not reported in retrieved text.
measures: navigation performance; spatial memory assessed via survey-based memory assessments
key_finding: Both the verbal and tonal navigational aids yielded slight navigational advantages and steep spatial memory costs despite presenting mixed spatial perspective instructions. The authors state that this equivalent impairment between information formats suggests navigational aids impair spatial memory by dividing attention rather than by selectively interfering with verbal working memory.
caveat_flags: abstract only; no numeric effect sizes reported; within-participants design

title: Navigational Aids and Spatial Memory Impairment: The Role of Divided Attention
design: Within-participants factorial design crossing aid presence and divided attention; navigation followed by spatial memory assessments
measures: not reported in retrieved text
key_finding: Divided attention alone impaired spatial memory. Navigational aid presence impaired spatial memory when attention was undivided, replicating previous findings, but did not to a greater extent when attention was divided. These findings suggest that navigational aids divide attention sufficiently to impair spatial memory.
caveat_flags: abstract only

title: Could Prolonged Usage of GPS Navigation Implemented in Augmented Reality Smart Glasses Affect Hippocampal Functional Connectivity?
design: Randomised? No; controlled longitudinal study comparing AR/GPS glasses group vs control group, pre/post 3 months
population: Healthy right-handed adults, Mean age (SD)=28.8 (7.1), 27 males and 6 females
exposure_duration: 3 months (10-12 weeks), M GPStime (SD) = 33 (7.2) hours; M GPSwalk (SD)=14.9 (8.8) h
measures: rsfMRI functional connectivity (seed-driven ROI-to-ROI, Fisher-transformed Z scores) of right/left hippocampus; Virtual City Task (pointing error, path efficiency, recall)
key_finding: The experimental group showed FC decrease after three months of using GPS navigation implemented in AR glasses in contrast to FC increase in the control group without such intervention. Importantly, no effect of intervention on navigational abilities was observed. We identified significant Spearman correlation coefficient between the duration of active usage of the AR glasses in head mounted mode and FC changes of the right HPC with the posterior portion of the left parahippocampal cortex (r HPC_r/pPaHC_l = 0.502, p = 0.040).
effect_size: Cohen's d values reported for FC changes ranging e.g. d=1.254 (HPC_right-pTFusC_l), d=1.189 (Cereb3_r), d=1.142 (pPaHC_l), d=0.966 (aPaHC_l), d=0.747 (Hippocampus_l/r); correlation r=0.502, p=0.040 (HPC_r/pPaHC_l); r=0.453, p=0.068 (HPC_r/HPC_l)
limitations: Intervention effects did not survive conservative multiple-comparison correction (p<0.05 uncorrected only); small sample size (pilot study); moderate/insufficient compliance with device usage due to technical problems; unbalanced baseline FC between groups due to non-random group assignment based on willingness to wear glasses; use of atlas-based ROI-to-ROI approach with averaging across functionally inhomogeneous areas; missing navigation records for control group
caveat_flags: non-randomised group assignment; small sample size; multiple comparisons uncorrected; self-report exposure measure (partly, also sensor logs); short intervention duration; low compliance/technical issues

title: Spatial knowledge impairment after GPS guided navigation: Eye-tracking study in a virtual town
design: not reported in retrieved text
measures: not reported in retrieved text
key_finding: Results show that the more time participants spend with the GPS-like map, the less accurate spatial knowledge they manifest and the longer paths they travel without GPS guidance. This poor performance cannot be explained by individual differences in cognitive skills. The amount of time spent with the GPS is related to participant's subjective evaluation of their own navigation skills, with less confident navigators using GPS more intensively.
caveat_flags: abstract only

title: Satellite Navigation and Geospatial Awareness: Long-Term Effects of Using Navigation Tools on Wayfinding and Spatial Orientation
design: Not randomised; correlational survey plus behavioral experiment comparing users with differing accumulated navigation-tool experience across tool types (mobile, paper map).
exposure_duration: Long-term; measured as regular use (time length and frequency) and accumulated experience (time length multiplied by frequency)
measures: Sense of direction, mental rotation, survey navigation strategy preference, travel efficiency, accuracy of learning route configurations
key_finding: Frequent users of pedestrian navigation systems tended to be low on sense of direction and mental rotation, whereas longtime users of maps tended to be high on sense of direction and favor survey navigation strategies. People with more accumulated experience of using in-car navigation systems traveled less efficiently and learned the configurations of traveled routes less accurately with a mobile tool and a paper map; structural equation modeling showed spatial aptitudes and accumulated experience independently affect wayfinding and spatial orientation, with the negative effects of accumulated experience larger than the positive effects of spatial aptitudes.
caveat_flags: abstract only; cross-sectional (survey component); self-report exposure measure

title: GPS use negatively affects environmental learning through spatial transformation abilities
design: not reported in retrieved text (appears correlational/model-based; no mention of randomisation or comparison groups)
measures: previously validated spatial transformation tasks (mental rotation, perspective-taking); environmental learning task (virtual environment); self-reported navigation ability
key_finding: The authors found that mental rotation and perspective-taking ability fully account for the effect of GPS use on learning of a virtual environment, and this relationship remained after controlling for existing navigation ability. They report that GPS use is negatively associated with perspective-taking indirectly through mental rotation, proposing that GPS use affects the transformation ability common to mental rotation and perspective-taking.
caveat_flags: abstract only; self-report exposure measure; cross-sectional (implied, not explicitly stated); abstract retrieved from the authors' PsyArXiv preprint record of the same title (10.31234/osf.io/qbgdr); the peer-reviewed J Environ Psychol version was not retrievable

title: Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation
design: Not randomised; cross-sectional correlational study (n=50) with a 3-year longitudinal follow-up subsample (n=13); GPS habits correlated with virtual navigation task performance.
population: Healthy young adults aged 19-35, right-handed regular drivers in Montreal, Canada; cross-sectional sample 18 women/32 men, mean age 27.6±4.5 years
exposure_duration: Lifetime GPS experience (hours); longitudinal: GPS use over 3.23±0.50 years between pre- and post-testing
measures: CSDLT (Concurrent Spatial Discrimination Learning Task) trials to criterion, probe 1, probe 2, probe 1+2 combined; 4/8 VM (4-on-8 Virtual Maze) trials to criterion, average learning errors, probe errors, map drawing score, navigation strategy score, average number of landmarks used, number of landmarks noticed; McGill GPS questionnaire (lifetime GPS experience, GPS reliance scale, sense of GPS dependence scale); SBSOD
key_finding: People with greater lifetime GPS experience have worse spatial memory during self-guided navigation, including a significant negative correlation with CSDLT probe 1 performance (r=−0.22, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.41, −0.01]) and a marginally significant negative correlation with both probe trials combined (r=−0.20, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.41, 0.01]), as well as significant negative correlations with 4/8 VM navigation strategy score (r=−0.20, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.38, −0.02]), map drawing score (r=−0.22, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.41, −0.02]), average number of landmarks used (r=−0.21, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.38, −0.05]), and number of landmarks noticed (r=−0.26, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.42, −0.09]). In the small longitudinal sample, greater GPS use since initial testing was associated with a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory (e.g., CSDLT probe 2: r=−0.68, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.91, −0.10]; map drawing: r=−0.52, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.79, −0.21]), and those who used GPS more did not do so because they felt they had a poor sense of direction (no significant correlation between lifetime GPS experience and SBSOD scores, r=0.07, Bootstrap BCa 95% CI [−0.16, 0.27]), suggesting that extensive GPS use led to a decline in spatial memory rather than the other way around.
caveat_flags: cross-sectional (primary analysis);small sample (longitudinal n=13);unplanned follow-up;correlational design (causality inferred, not established);self-report exposure measure (GPS questionnaire)

title: Wayfinding and acquisition of spatial knowledge with navigation assistance.
design: not reported in retrieved text whether randomised; comparison between visualization types (self-to-targets vs. comprehensive maps) and aligned vs. misaligned conditions.
measures: Wayfinding accuracy; self-to-object knowledge assessed with pointing tasks; object-to-object knowledge assessed with an allocentric configurational task; individual differences in perspective taking ability
key_finding: Alignment (rotations of the visualization according to changes of heading in the environment) appeared supportive for the acquisition of self-to-object knowledge with self-to-targets visualizations, but alignment was not effective with comprehensive maps. Wayfinding was impeded if visualizations were not aligned with the current heading, and individual differences in perspective taking ability played a strong role for wayfinding accuracy with misaligned visualizations.
caveat_flags: abstract only

title: An exploratory real-world wayfinding experiment: A comparison of drivers’ spatial learning with a paper map vs. turn-by-turn audiovisual route guidance
design: Randomised: two random groups compared, paper map vs turn-by-turn audiovisual route guidance, real-world driving task.
population: Car drivers driving their own vehicles to a predesignated destination in an unfamiliar residential neighborhood.
measures: Orientation (deviation in direction), landmark recognition, route recognition (error percentage) via spatial knowledge tests administered after the drive.
key_finding: The scores of map-assisted drivers were uncorrelated and, on average, higher in orientation (deviation in direction), landmark recognition and route recognition (error percentage). The landmark recognition scores of drivers assisted by TBT route guidance were significantly lower with a very large effect size. The route recognition scores of drivers assisted by route guidance showed strong correlations with orientation and with landmark recognition scores.
effect_size: very large effect size (landmark recognition, TBT vs map); exact statistic not reported in retrieved text
caveat_flags: abstract only; small sample not reported; self-report exposure measure not applicable

title: Rethinking GPS navigation: creating cognitive maps through auditory clues
design: Randomized within groups (Expert/Naïve) to Turn-by-turn vs Beacon condition; between-subjects comparison
population: Adults (mean age 33.8, SD 8.21); Microsoft employees (Experts) and interns (Naïve)
measures: Pointing task error (degrees) from Location A and novel Location B; map-drawing POI location error (distance in meters/pixels); route overlap; distance traveled
key_finding: The Naïve Beacon group was significantly better than the Naïve Turn-by-turn group at post-test pointing from Location A (Tukey's post-hoc), and condition showed a significant main effect on pointing accuracy from novel Location B (F(1,49)=5.01, p<0.05) and on map-drawing accuracy (F(1,49)=7.3, p<0.01). The authors state that 'the Naïve Beacon group demonstrated a more accurate spatial representation of the Microsoft campus' while Experts showed 'little differences between the conditions.'
effect_size: F(1,49)=6.2, p<0.05 (interaction, post-test pointing A); F(1,49)=4.41, p<0.05 (main effect condition, post-test pointing A); F(1,49)=5.01, p<0.05 (condition, Location B); F(1,49)=7.3, p<0.01 (condition, map task)
limitations: Small sample sizes per group (ideally 80 total per power analysis assuming d=0.5); Turn-by-turn group received verbal directions from experimenter rather than an actual navigation app; study area limited to walking paths, not roads, so may not generalize to car navigation
caveat_flags: small sample; non-standard exposure delivery (experimenter-given verbal turn-by-turn instead of app); single-session; convenience sample of employees/interns

title: Online mobile map effect: how smartphone map use impairs spatial memory
design: Comparison of smartphone map vs paper map route learning; randomisation not stated in retrieved text.
measures: Route retracing performance, state anxiety, confidence ratings
key_finding: The use of a smartphone map impaired spatial learning and knowledge acquisition; participants learned a route less accurately when they used a smartphone map than when using a paper map, revealed by a worse route retracing performance. Although navigation accuracy decreased for the second, unaided walk after the first walk aided with a smartphone map, participants' self-evaluation in terms of state anxiety and confidence ratings did not show a statistically significant difference, suggesting smartphone map users did not perceive the memory impairment caused by the smartphone map use.
caveat_flags: abstract only

title: GPS use and navigation ability: A systematic review and meta-analysis
design: Not randomised; meta-analysis/narrative synthesis of 23 studies comparing GPS use vs. non-use/associations with navigation ability.
measures: environmental knowledge, sense of direction (self-reported), wayfinding
key_finding: The narrative synthesis presented negative associations between GPS use and performance in environmental knowledge and self-reported sense of direction measures and a positive association with wayfinding. When considering quantitative data, results revealed a negative effect of GPS use on environmental knowledge (r = −.18 [95% CI: −.28, −.08]) and sense of direction (r = −.25 [95% CI: −.39, −.12]) and a positive yet not significant effect on wayfinding (r = .07 [95% CI: −.28, .41]).
effect_size: Environmental knowledge: r = −.18 [95% CI: −.28, −.08]; Sense of direction: r = −.25 [95% CI: −.39, −.12]; Wayfinding: r = .07 [95% CI: −.28, .41]
limitations: Current literature has several strengths but also methodological weaknesses that limit the quality of evidence, with 69% of the studies classified with a moderate to high risk of bias.
caveat_flags: STUDY TYPE: meta-analysis; abstract only; meta-analysis of heterogeneous studies; self-report exposure measure (sense of direction); risk of bias moderate-to-high in 69% of studies; non-significant CI for wayfinding

title: How is GPS used? Understanding navigation system use and its relation to spatial ability
design: Not randomised; correlational/cross-sectional survey study (two studies, online n=188 and in-person n=61, combined n=249) relating self-reported GPS use/dependency to self-report and objective navigation measures.
population: Online study: ages 18–29 (M=19.54, SD=1.47, 135 females), UCSB Psychology Research participant pool. In-person study: ages 18–32 (M=19.67, SD=2.63, 30 females).
measures: GPS Dependency Scale; GPS Usage scale (turn-by-turn, route planning, time/traffic estimates, finding a specific service); Santa Barbara Sense of Direction (SBSOD) scale; Spatial Anxiety scale; Exploration Tendency scale; Navigational Growth Mindset scale; Social Desirability Scale; Mental Rotation Test (MRT); Virtual SILCton task (onsite pointing within-route and between-route, map reconstruction); Spatial Orientation Test (SOT, perspective-taking).
key_finding: Reported GPS dependence was negatively correlated with objective navigation performance, r(59) = −0.34, p = 0.008, 99% CI [−0.60, −0.01], and with self-reported sense of direction, r(247) = −0.56, p < 0.001, 99.9% CI [−0.69, −0.40], and positively correlated with spatial anxiety, r(247) = 0.43, p < 0.001, 99.9% CI [0.25, 0.59]. Greater reported use of GPS for turn-by-turn directions was associated with a poorer sense of direction, 99.9% CI [−0.61, −0.28], and higher spatial anxiety, 99.9% CI [0.14, 0.51], while correlations between reported use of specific GPS functions and objective navigation performance did not reach statistical significance (e.g., turn-by-turn: r(59) = −0.23, p = 0.071). People reported using GPS most frequently for time and traffic estimates (M = 1.21) regardless of ability, and reported using GPS less as familiarity with an environment increased, regardless of ability.
effect_size: GPS dependency vs SOD: r(247) = −0.56, p < 0.001, 99.9% CI [−0.69, −0.40]; GPS dependency vs spatial anxiety: r(247) = 0.43, p < 0.001, 99.9% CI [0.25, 0.59]; GPS dependency vs objective navigation (SILCton): r(59) = −0.34, p = 0.008, 99% CI [−0.60, −0.01]; turn-by-turn GPS vs SOD: 99.9% CI [−0.61, −0.28]; turn-by-turn GPS vs spatial anxiety: 99.9% CI [0.14, 0.51]; one-way ANOVA for GPS function frequency: F(3,741) = 47.33, p < 0.001, η² = 0.07.
caveat_flags: cross-sectional; self-report exposure measure; correlational (no causal inference); small sample for objective navigation measure (n=61); online sample restricted age range (18-29) and student pool

title: Video gaming, but not reliance on GPS, is associated with spatial navigation performance
design: Not randomised; correlational, cross-sectional study using multiple linear regression comparing GPS reliance and video gaming hours against wayfinding performance.
population: US-based participants, mean age = 26.3 years, range = 18-52 years
measures: Wayfinding performance measured via the mobile app Sea Hero Quest; self-reported questions on reliance on GPS and video game experience (weekly hours of video gaming)
key_finding: A multiple linear regression model found no significant association between reliance on GPS and wayfinding performance. There was a significant association between weekly hours of video gaming and wayfinding performance.
caveat_flags: cross-sectional; self-report exposure measure; abstract only

title: How Do In-Car Navigation Aids Impair Expert Navigators’ Spatial Learning Ability?
venue: Annals of the American Association of Geographers
design: Between-participants, non-randomised; low-dependence vs high-dependence taxi drivers compared
population: 24 male expert taxi drivers in Beijing
exposure_duration: 8.17 years average past use; learning phase videos 2 minutes each
measures: Scene recognition accuracy, route recognition accuracy, sketch map r2/scaling bias/rotational bias, eye movement (fixation count, saccade count, average fixation duration), EEG frontal theta relative PSD
key_finding: Scene recognition accuracy of the LD group was significantly better than that of the HD group (H=5.57, p=0.02, η2=0.13); a significant difference in scaling bias was found between LD and HD groups (H=4.03, p=0.045, η2=0.10), indicating LD participants could better estimate interlandmark distance; no significant differences were found in route recognition accuracy, r2, or rotational bias.
effect_size: H=5.57, p=0.02, η2=0.13 (scene recognition); H=4.03, p=0.045, η2=0.10 (scaling bias); theta PSD difference p=0.03, η2=0.41 (second trial, Fz)
caveat_flags: cross-sectional; small sample; between-subjects design; self-report exposure measure; all-male sample; cross-sectional comparison of habitual heavy vs light users; small sample (n=24); males only

title: The Effects of Non‐CAS Graphing Calculators on Student Achievement and Attitude Levels in Mathematics: A Meta‐Analysis
design: Meta-analysis of 42 studies comparing students with vs without graphing calculator access during instruction; randomisation not reported in retrieved text.
population: Middle and high school mathematics students, and college students through first semester calculus
measures: Achievement (procedural, conceptual, and overall) and attitude levels in mathematics
key_finding: When calculators were part of instruction but not testing, students' benefited from using calculators while developing the skills necessary to understand mathematics concepts. When calculators were included in testing and instruction, the procedural, conceptual, and overall achievement skills of students improved.
caveat_flags: STUDY TYPE: meta-analysis; abstract only; meta-analysis; mixed population including minors; no numeric effect sizes reported; inclusion overridden by reviewer: meta-analysis spanning middle/high school AND college courses; not children-only

title: Performance Consequences of Automation-Induced 'Complacency'
venue: The International Journal of Aviation Psychology
design: Two experiments; within-subjects manipulation of automation reliability (constant low, constant high, variable); randomisation not reported in retrieved text.
measures: Operator detection of automation failures in a system-monitoring task under automation control; also tested with system monitoring as the only task
key_finding: Operator detection of automation failures was substantially worse for constant-reliability than for variable-reliability automation after about 20 min under automation control, indicating that the former condition induced "complacency." When system monitoring was the only task, detection was very efficient and was unaffected by variations in automation reliability. The results provide the first empirical evidence of the performance consequences of automation-induced "complacency."
caveat_flags: abstract only

title: Computer Decision Support as a Source of Interpretation Error: The Case of Electrocardiograms
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
design: Randomized controlled trial, two-period crossover design, matched pairs; compared EKG interpretation accuracy with vs without computer interpretation.
measures: Subjects' interpretive accuracy of discrete, cardiologist-determined EKG findings, judged by a board-certified internist
key_finding: Without the CI, subjects interpreted 48.9% (95% confidence interval, 45.0% to 52.8%) of the findings correctly; with the CI, subjects interpreted 55.4% (51.9% to 58.9%) correctly (p < 0.0001). Subjects erroneously agreed with the incorrect CI more often when it was presented with the EKG 67.7% (57.2% to 76.7%) than when it was not 34.6% (23.8% to 47.3%; p < 0.0001), and accuracy dropped to 48.3% (40.4% to 56.4%) when the incorrect computer advice was provided (p = 0.131) compared to 56.7% (48.5% to 64.5%) when not provided. The authors conclude that computer decision support systems can generally improve interpretive accuracy, but subjects were influenced significantly by incorrect advice, which tempers the overall usefulness of computer-generated advice.
effect_size: Without CI: 48.9% (45.0%-52.8%); With CI: 55.4% (51.9%-58.9%), p < 0.0001; Correct CI included: 68.1% (63.2%-72.7%) vs 53.1% (47.7%-58.5%) not included, p < 0.0001; Incorrect CI provided: 48.3% (40.4%-56.4%) vs not provided 56.7% (48.5%-64.5%), p = 0.131; Erroneous agreement with incorrect CI: 67.7% (57.2%-76.7%) presented vs 34.6% (23.8%-47.3%) not presented, p < 0.0001
caveat_flags: abstract only; laboratory setting

title: The relationship between manual handling performance and recent flying experience in air transport pilots
design: not reported in retrieved text
measures: flight path tracking measures; frequency-based control strategy measures
key_finding: Significant relationships are identified between pilots' very recent flying experience and their manual control strategy. The study demonstrates a novel application of frequency analysis, which produces a broader and more sensitive analysis of pilot performance than has been offered in previous research.
caveat_flags: abstract only; inclusion overridden by reviewer: in scope: unaided manual handling performance vs recent flying experience

title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators
venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
design: Systematic review of literature across research fields; not randomised; not a single study comparison but synthesis of 74 included studies.
measures: not reported in retrieved text
key_finding: Although most research shows overall improved performance with use of clinical decision support systems, there is often a failure to recognize the new errors that CDSS can introduce. User factors (cognitive style, DSS, task-specific experience), attitudinal factors (trust and confidence), and environmental mediators (workload, task complexity, time constraint) mediated automation bias, while implementation factors (training, user accountability) and DSS design factors (advice position, updated confidence levels, information vs recommendation) acted as mitigators.
caveat_flags: STUDY TYPE: systematic review; abstract only; review of heterogeneous fields not limited to healthcare; exposure not clearly non-AI tool; inclusion overridden by reviewer: systematic review; outcome measured WITH the aid (automation bias), flagged

title: How to Discriminate between Computer-Aided and Computer-Hindered Decisions
design: Reanalysis of prior study data; not stated as randomised; within-reader comparison of mammogram interpretation with vs without CAD.
population: professionals ("readers") interpreting mammograms for cancer screening
measures: sensitivity (probability of correct screening decision on a patient with cancer), cancer difficulty (proportion of readers who missed it), reader discriminating ability (Youden's determinant)
key_finding: Use of CAD was associated with a 0.016 increase in sensitivity (95% CI, 0.003-0.028) for the 44 least discriminating radiologists for 45 relatively easy, mostly CAD-detected cancers. However, for the 6 most discriminating radiologists, with CAD, sensitivity decreased by 0.145 (95% CI, 0.034-0.257) for the 15 relatively difficult cancers. The authors conclude that despite the original study detecting no significant average effect, CAD helped the less discriminating readers but hindered the more discriminating readers.
effect_size: 0.016 increase in sensitivity (95% CI, 0.003-0.028) for 44 least discriminating radiologists; 0.145 decrease in sensitivity (95% CI, 0.034-0.257) for 6 most discriminating radiologists
caveat_flags: abstract only; secondary reanalysis of existing data; exploratory analysis; small subgroup (n=6 most discriminating radiologists); not randomised; no significant average effect in original study

title: The Retention of Manual Flying Skills in the Automated Cockpit
venue: Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
design: Simulator study; automation level systematically varied within pilots; not stated as randomised; performance graded and pilots probed on thoughts.
measures: instrument scanning, manual control skills, performance on manual cognitive flight tasks (tracking aircraft position without map display, deciding navigational steps, recognizing instrument system failures), frequency of task-unrelated thought
key_finding: Pilots' instrument scanning and manual control skills were mostly intact, even when pilots reported that they were infrequently practiced. However, when pilots were asked to manually perform the cognitive tasks needed for manual flight, more frequent and significant problems were observed, and performance on these cognitive tasks was associated with measures of how often pilots engaged in task-unrelated thought when cockpit automation was used.
caveat_flags: abstract only; small sample; simulator study; non-randomised automation manipulation; self-report exposure measure

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Digital Screening Mammography With and Without Computer-Aided Detection
design: Observational, not randomised; compared digital mammography interpretation with vs without CAD, including a subset of 107 radiologists who did both.
n: 323 973 women; 495 818 mammograms interpreted with CAD vs 129 807 without CAD; 271 radiologists from 66 facilities; 3159 breast cancers identified.
population: Women undergoing digital screening mammography in US community practice, 2003 through 2009, within the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium.
measures: Sensitivity, specificity, screen-detected and interval cancers per 1000 women (cancer detection rate), modeled via logistic regression with radiologist-specific random effects; conditional logistic regression for intraradiologist comparison.
key_finding: Screening performance was not improved with CAD on any metric assessed. Mammography sensitivity was 85.3% (95% CI, 83.6%-86.9%) with and 87.3% (95% CI, 84.5%-89.7%) without CAD, while specificity was 91.6% (95% CI, 91.0%-92.2%) with and 91.4% (95% CI, 90.6%-92.0%) without CAD, with no difference in cancer detection rate (4.1 in 1000 women screened with and without CAD). Among radiologists who interpreted both with and without CAD, sensitivity was significantly decreased with CAD (odds ratio, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.29-0.97), and CAD did not improve intraradiologist performance.
effect_size: Sensitivity: 85.3% (95% CI, 83.6%-86.9%) with CAD vs 87.3% (95% CI, 84.5%-89.7%) without CAD; Specificity: 91.6% (95% CI, 91.0%-92.2%) with vs 91.4% (95% CI, 90.6%-92.0%) without CAD; cancer detection rate 4.1 in 1000 women both groups; odds ratio for sensitivity in intraradiologist subset, 0.53 (95% CI, 0.29-0.97).
caveat_flags: abstract only; observational/non-randomised design; possible confounding by indication or facility/radiologist selection not detailed

title: Flying the Needles
venue: Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
design: Not randomised; cross-sectional comparison of four naturally occurring pilot groups by fleet (short-/long-haul) and rank.
population: 126 randomly selected airline pilots, assigned to four equal groups by fleet (short-haul, long-haul) and rank (first officer, captain)
measures: Average ILS deviation scores during a manual flight scenario with a raw data precision approach
key_finding: Average ILS deviation scores differed significantly in relation to the group assignments, and the strongest predictor variable was fleet, indicating degraded performance among long-haul pilots. The authors conclude that recent flight practice is a significantly stronger predictor for fine-motor flying performance than the time period since flight school or even the total or type-specific flight experience.
caveat_flags: abstract only; cross-sectional; exposure not experimentally manipulated (natural fleet/rank grouping); no numeric effect sizes reported

title: I spy with my little eye: Analysis of airline pilots’ gaze patterns in a manual instrument flight scenario
design: Non-randomised between-groups comparison of short-haul vs long-haul pilots performing a manual approach; no randomisation reported.
population: Airline pilots, differing by practice level (short-haul vs. long-haul)
measures: Eye-tracking derived gaze patterns/saccade groupings; manual flight performance during a manual raw data precision approach
key_finding: The analysis of gaze patterns, based on predominant saccades, revealed one main group of saccades among long-haul pilots, whereas short-haul pilots showed more balanced scanning using two different groups of saccades. Short-haul pilots generally demonstrated better manual flight performance, and within this group one type of scan pattern was found to facilitate the manual landing task more; long-haul pilots tend to utilize visual scanning behaviors that are inappropriate for the manual ILS landing task.
caveat_flags: abstract only; non-randomised group comparison; no effect sizes or sample size reported

title: Evaluation of Cognitive Skill Degradation in Flight Planning
venue: Journal of Cognitive Engineering and Decision Making
design: Two studies: cognitive task analysis, then empirical evaluation with three groups (manual, alternating, automation-only) across practice trials; randomisation not reported in retrieved text.
exposure_duration: Trials separated by 2 weeks; three practice trials for alternating/automation groups
measures: not reported in retrieved text
key_finding: The automation group showed the most performance degradation and highest workload, while the manual group showed the least performance degradation and least workload. Automation use did not provide the practice needed to mitigate cognitive skill degradation.

title: A role for metamemory in cognitive offloading

The winning computational model showed beliefs about the performance boost from offloaded information were negatively coupled to evaluations of memory ability, and confidence judgments predicted decisions to use saved information, indicating cognitive offloading is associated with metacognitive evaluation about memory performance.

caveat_flags: self-report exposure measure (confidence ratings); small sample (Experiments 1 and 2a n=27); within-subject design limits generalisability; monetary incentive structure may not generalise to real-world offloading behaviour

title: Offloading items from memory: individual differences in cognitive offloading in a short-term memory task
design: Not randomised (blocked, order counterbalanced); within-subjects comparison of choice (offloading allowed) vs no-choice (internal memory only) conditions; correlational individual-differences analyses.
population: University students (undergraduates receiving course credit), final sample from two sites (California State University, Sacramento, and Stony Brook University); data collected from 130, 16 excluded, final n=114.
measures: Auditory short-term memory task (letter recall, set sizes 2,4,6,8,10) scored all-or-none for accuracy in no-choice and choice conditions; proportion of trials offloaded (written down) in choice block; working memory capacity (WMC) composite from automated operation span and symmetry span (Z-score composite using Redick et al. 2012 norms).
key_finding: Offloading conferred a performance advantage over relying on internal memory, particularly at higher memory loads: significant main effect of condition (F(1,113)=96.539, p<.001, η2G=0.105) with better performance in choice than no-choice, and a significant condition × load interaction (F(4,452)=42.478, p<.001, η2G=0.085) where the load effect was less pronounced in the choice condition. However, contrary to Risko and Dunn (2015), no-choice block performance was not correlated with offloading frequency (r(112)=-0.012, p=.897), and WMC did not predict offloading behavior (model with no-choice performance and WMC: R2=0.001, adjusted R2=-0.017, F(2,111)=0.066, p=.936) nor the benefit of offloading at high loads (t(111)=0.821, p=.414), while proportion of high-load trials offloaded was a significant predictor of offloading benefit (t(111)=4.349, p<.001).
effect_size: Main effect of condition: F(1,113)=96.539, p<.001, η2G=0.105; condition × load interaction: F(4,452)=42.478, p<.001, η2G=0.085; set size 2: t(38)=-2.647, p=.012, d=-0.535; set size 4: t(68)=0.910, p=.366, d=0.115; set size 6: t(100)=6.278, p<.001, d=0.729; set size 8: t(104)=12.113, p<.001, d=1.478; set size 10: t(107)=9.672, p<.001, d=1.312; no-choice performance × offloading correlation: r(112)=-0.012, p=.897; regression model with no-choice+WMC: R2=0.001, adjusted R2=-0.017, F(2,111)=0.066, p=.936; high-load benefit model: R2=0.148, adjusted R2=0.132, F(2,111)=9.619, p<.001, offloading proportion t(111)=4.349, p<.001, WMC t(111)=0.821, p=.414.
limitations: Lower overall accuracy compared to Risko and Dunn (2015), possibly due to sample differences (higher proportion of non-native English speakers), compensation differences (course credit only vs. course credit or pay), auditory-only stimulus presentation difficulties, and inability to isolate error sources on offloaded trials (incorrect/incomplete copying vs. reporting errors).
caveat_flags: registered report; replication study; correlational individual-differences analyses; auditory-only stimuli; sample differences from original study noted by authors; null findings for key hypotheses

title: Consequences of cognitive offloading: Boosting performance but diminishing memory

title: Google effects on memory: a meta-analytical review of the media effects of intensive Internet search behavior
design: Meta-analysis (random-effects model) of 35 independent comparisons from 22 studies; not a single randomised trial; comparisons vary by included primary study (e.g., experimental vs. control groups, pre/post Internet search training).
n: 30,889 participants across 22 selected articles (35 independent comparisons); ages ranging from 12 to 89 years old.
population: Participants across 22 studies, ages 12 to 89 years old; region categorized as North America, Europe, or Asia; not reported in retrieved text whether restricted to any specific population beyond this.
measures: Cohen's d as the effect size metric; five categories of research type: cognitive load, cognitive measurement, behavioral phenotype, cognitive self-esteem, and psychophysiology (e.g., EEG, fMRI); Cochrane Q statistic and I2 index for heterogeneity; moderator analyses (region, publication year, percentage of males, age, sample size, type).
key_finding: The authors found that google effects is closely associated with cognitive load, behavioral phenotype and cognitive self-esteem. For the cognitive load subgroup, observed outcome = 0.73, 95%CI = [0.22, 1.24]; behavioral phenotype subgroup observed outcome = 0.39, 95%CI = [0.16, 0.61]; cognitive self-esteem subgroup observed outcome = 0.91, 95%CI = [0.23, 1.59]. For cognitive measurement, observed outcome = 0.56, 95%CI = [−0.15, 1.28], and psychophysiology, observed outcome = 1.01, 95%CI = [−0.12, 2.13], the 95%CI included zero so it was not possible to conclude whether these factors had a significant effect. Meta-analyses show that participants in North America (parameter = −1.0365, 95%CI = [−1.8758, −0.1972], p < 0.05) are more susceptible to frequent Internet search behavior relative to other regions, and region (Q = 6.1997, p < 0.050) accounted for 13.18% of the total heterogeneity.
effect_size: Cohen's d ranged from −0.85 to 4.38 across included studies; subgroup observed outcomes: cognitive load 0.73 [0.22, 1.24]; behavioral phenotype 0.39 [0.16, 0.61]; cognitive self-esteem 0.91 [0.23, 1.59]; cognitive measurement 0.56 [−0.15, 1.28]; psychophysiology 1.01 [−0.12, 2.13]; region moderator: Europe d = −1.1063, 95%CI = [−2.3157, 0.103]; North America d = −1.0365*, 95%CI = [−1.8758, −0.1972] (*p < 0.05); the pooled d overall was described as 'a moderate but statistically significant effect size' without a specific numeric value reported in retrieved text.
limitations: Lack of solicitation for ongoing or unpublished studies, potentially missing relevant research; some moderators may have been neglected during coding; region analysis could be optimized further (e.g., country-specific data); funnel plots used for publication bias but potential sources of bias may still exist, and additional tests like Trim-and-Fill were not employed in this study.
caveat_flags: STUDY TYPE: meta-analysis; meta-analysis of heterogeneous primary designs; substantial heterogeneity across studies; wide age range pooled together; region moderator based on limited categories (only Europe and North America significant); some subgroup CIs cross zero; self-report exposure measure in some underlying studies (not fully specified in retrieved text); english-language restriction; published studies only (no unpublished/grey literature)

title: The Effects of Automatic Spelling Correction Software on Understanding and Comprehension in Compensated Dyslexia: Improved Recall Following Dictation

key_finding: We confirm impaired working memory in a sample of university students with (compensated) dyslexia, and using a within‐subject design with three test conditions, we show that these participants demonstrated better understanding of a piece of text if they had used automatic spelling correction software during a dictation/transcription task. title: Use of predictive text in text messaging over the course of a year and its relationship with spelling, orthographic processing and grammar

measures: Use of text abbreviations ('textisms'), genuine spelling errors, grammatical violations/errors in text messages, orthographic processing, morphological awareness, grammatical understanding, consistency of predictive text use over time.
key_finding: No differences in use of textisms were found between predictive text users and nonusers, but secondary school children who used predictive text made more genuine spelling errors than nonusers. Consistency of predictive text use was unrelated to grammatical understanding, spelling or orthographic processing for primary and secondary school cohorts, and predictive text use was negatively related to morphological awareness for adult participants.
